**Moonlight Sonata**
Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor (Op. 27, No. 2), subtitled "quasi una fantasia." Its slow first movement (Adagio sostenuto) is built on soft, repeated triplet arpeggios and is marked "senza sordino," which means the damper pedal is held down throughout. The critic Ludwig Rellstab compared the movement to moonlight reflecting on Lake Lucerne, which gave the piece its nickname. Its third movement is a stormy Presto agitato of rising C-sharp minor arpeggios. Liszt called the middle movement "a flower between two abysses."

**32 piano sonatas**
Beethoven's set of 32 piano sonatas is a cornerstone of the repertoire, and Artur Schnabel made the first complete recording of it. Nicknamed sonatas include the "Pathétique," "Moonlight," "Waldstein" (No. 21, dedicated to Count Waldstein), "Appassionata," and "Les Adieux" (No. 26). The "Les Adieux" sonata has three movements, "The Farewell," "The Absence," and "The Return," and the syllables "Le-be-wohl" are written over its first three chords.

**"Ode to Joy"**
Friedrich Schiller's poem, which Beethoven set in the choral finale of his Ninth Symphony. The text praises a "spark of divinity" and "daughter of Elysium" and celebrates universal brotherhood. The bass soloist first enters with the recitative "O friends, not these tones!" In 1989, Leonard Bernstein conducted the symphony to celebrate the fall of the Berlin Wall, changing the word "Freude" (joy) to "Freiheit" (freedom).

**Symphony No. 9 ("Choral")**
Beethoven's final symphony, in D minor, which he wrote while almost completely deaf. It unusually puts the scherzo second and adds four vocal soloists and a chorus in the finale, which also includes a "Turkish march." His earlier Choral Fantasy anticipated its finale. Wagner chose it to celebrate the laying of the Bayreuth Festspielhaus foundation stone in 1872.

**1824 premiere of the Ninth Symphony**
The symphony premiered in 1824 at Vienna's Kärntnertor Theater, with Michael Umlauf as the actual conductor. The deaf Beethoven stood beating time and had to be turned around to see the audience applauding. The soloists included Henriette Sontag and Caroline Unger, and the concert also included the Consecration of the House Overture.

**Symphony No. 5**
Beethoven's C minor symphony (Op. 67). It opens with the "short-short-short-long" motif that is often described as "fate knocking at the door." The scherzo leads without a pause (attacca) into a triumphant C major finale, which adds piccolo, contrabassoon, and three trombones and ends with a long run of C major chords.

**Eroica Symphony**
Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major. It opens with two forte E-flat chords, includes a C minor funeral march as its second movement, and is often called the start of musical Romanticism. Beethoven scratched out its dedication to Napoleon after Napoleon crowned himself emperor, and replaced it with "composed to celebrate the memory of a great man." The finale's variations use the same contredanse theme as his Eroica Variations, Op. 35.

**Pathétique Sonata**
Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, dedicated to Prince Karl Lichnowsky. Its first movement alternates a slow Grave introduction with a fast Allegro di molto e con brio, and its Adagio cantabile second movement has a famous A-flat major theme. Elgar said the opening of "Nimrod" was a "hint" of this Adagio. C minor is often called Beethoven's most dramatic key.

**Für Elise**
Beethoven's Bagatelle No. 25 in A minor, dedicated to an unidentified "Elise." It begins with the right hand alternating E and D-sharp, and it is one of the most popular pieces for piano students.

**Hammerklavier Sonata**
Piano Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major, which opens with fortissimo B-flat major chords. It ends with a huge three-voice fugue whose subject begins with a leaping tenth. It was long considered unplayable until Franz Liszt performed it in public.

**Piano Sonata No. 32 and its "Arietta"**
Beethoven's final piano sonata, in C minor, has only two movements and is dedicated to Archduke Rudolf. Its second movement, the "Arietta," is a set of variations in time signatures such as 9/16 and 12/32, and its syncopated rhythms led the pianist Jeremy Denk to call it "proto-jazz."

**Pastoral Symphony**
Beethoven's Symphony No. 6, a programmatic work depicting country life. Its second movement, "Scene by the Brook," ends with woodwinds imitating a nightingale, a quail, and a cuckoo. A fourth-movement "Thunderstorm," the only movement that uses timpani, interrupts the "Merry Gathering of Country Folk."

**String quartets**
Beethoven's quartets include the three "Razumovsky" quartets, the "Harp" and "Serioso" quartets, and six late quartets. The late quartets include the seven-movement C-sharp minor quartet, Op. 131, and the A minor quartet, Op. 132, whose slow movement in the Lydian mode is the "Heiliger Dankgesang." The Grosse Fuge was originally the finale of the Op. 130 quartet.

**Heiligenstadt Testament**
A letter Beethoven wrote in 1802 to his brothers, in which he despairs over his growing deafness but resolves to keep living for the sake of his art. It is often linked to the beginning of his heroic "middle period," including the Eroica.

**An die ferne Geliebte**
"To the Distant Beloved," a set of six songs often considered the first true song cycle. The songs are played without a break, and the cycle ends by returning to the melody of the first song. Beethoven's other vocal works include the song "Adelaide" and his only opera, Fidelio, which features the "Prisoners' Chorus."
